title: Lecture 1: Introduction to Software Engineering and Object-Oriented Fundamentals
summary: This foundational lecture introduces modern software engineering principles and the critical role of object technology in building high-quality industrial software systems. Students will explore the challenges of contemporary software development, understand essential quality attributes (correctness, robustness, extendibility, reusability), and learn fundamental object-oriented programming concepts including classes, objects, and encapsulation. The lecture establishes the course framework and introduces Eiffel notation as the practical vehicle for learning.
learningObjectives: Articulate the key challenges in modern software engineering and explain why systematic approaches are necessary for industrial-scale systems
Define and distinguish between the four critical quality attributes: correctness, robustness, extendibility, and reusability
Explain the fundamental concepts of object-oriented programming and why object technology is the approach of choice for high-quality systems
Describe the relationship between classes and objects, and explain the principle of encapsulation
Recognize basic Eiffel notation and understand its role in expressing object-oriented concepts
Understand the course structure, assessment components, and learning trajectory for the semester

sections.title: Quality Attributes: The Foundation of Software Excellence
learningGoals: Define and distinguish the four critical quality attributes
Understand why quality must be designed in, not tested in
Recognize trade-offs between different quality attributes

subsections.title: Correctness: Does the Software Do What It Should?
keyPoints: Definition: Ability to perform exact tasks as defined by specification
Correctness is absolute: software either meets spec or doesn't
Formal specifications vs. informal requirements
Verification and validation approaches
Correctness as the most fundamental quality attribute
examples: Banking system: transferring exactly the specified amount between accounts
Medical device: delivering precise dosage as prescribed
Compiler: generating code that faithfully implements source semantics
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Venn diagram showing specification space vs. implementation behavior, with correctness as complete overlap

subsections.title: Robustness: Graceful Handling of Abnormal Conditions
keyPoints: Definition: Ability to react appropriately to abnormal conditions
Difference between correctness (normal cases) and robustness (exceptional cases)
Error handling, exception management, defensive programming
Fail-safe vs. fail-secure approaches
User experience during error conditions
examples: Web server handling malformed HTTP requests without crashing
Text editor auto-saving work when system runs out of memory
Database system maintaining consistency despite power failure
Mobile app providing meaningful error messages for network timeouts
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Flowchart showing normal execution path vs. exception handling paths with recovery mechanisms

subsections.title: Extendibility: Adapting to Change
keyPoints: Definition: Ease of adapting software to changes in specification
Change is inevitable in software systems
Modular design and separation of concerns
Impact analysis: localized vs. ripple effects of changes
Design for change from the beginning
examples: E-commerce system adding new payment methods without restructuring checkout
Game engine supporting new character types through inheritance
Report generator adding new output formats via plugin architecture
Tax calculation software adapting to new tax laws through configuration
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Before/after comparison showing well-designed system (localized change) vs. poorly-designed system (cascading changes)

subsections.title: Reusability: Leveraging Existing Solutions
keyPoints: Definition: Ability to use software elements in multiple applications
Economic benefits: reduce development time and cost
Libraries, frameworks, and components
Generality vs. specificity trade-offs
Reusability requires upfront investment in design
examples: Standard library collections (lists, sets, maps) used across thousands of applications
Authentication module reused across multiple enterprise applications
UI component library shared across product family
Mathematical algorithms packaged for multiple domains
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Pyramid showing reusability spectrum from application-specific code to widely-reusable libraries

subsections.title: Quality Attributes Interplay
keyPoints: Quality attributes can reinforce or conflict with each other
Extendibility and reusability often go hand-in-hand
Performance vs. extendibility trade-offs
Correctness and robustness as complementary properties
Object-oriented design supports all four quality attributes
examples: Highly optimized code may sacrifice extendibility for performance
Generic reusable components may be harder to verify for correctness
Robust error handling adds complexity but improves reliability
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Matrix showing positive and negative interactions between quality attributes

exercises: For a system you know well (e.g., email client), rate it on each quality attribute and justify your ratings
Design a simple stack data structure: identify one design decision that affects each quality attribute

sections.title: Object-Oriented Programming Fundamentals
learningGoals: Understand why object technology is the approach of choice for quality software
Grasp the fundamental concepts of classes and objects
Explain encapsulation and information hiding principles

subsections.title: Why Object Technology?
keyPoints: Object-oriented programming as established approach for high-quality systems
Natural modeling of real-world entities and relationships
Support for all four quality attributes through OO mechanisms
Industry adoption and ecosystem maturity
Evolution from procedural to object-oriented paradigms
examples: Modeling a university system: students, courses, enrollments as objects
GUI frameworks: buttons, windows, menus as objects with behavior
Simulation systems: agents, environments as interacting objects
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Comparison table: procedural vs. object-oriented approaches for the same problem domain

subsections.title: Classes: Templates for Objects
keyPoints: Class as a blueprint or template defining structure and behavior
Attributes (data) and methods (operations) as class members
Class as a type in the type system
Abstract data types and implementation hiding
Class as unit of modularity and reuse
examples: BANK_ACCOUNT class with balance attribute and deposit/withdraw methods
POINT class with x, y coordinates and distance calculation method
STUDENT class with name, ID, grades and GPA calculation method
subsections.suggestedDiagram: UML class diagram showing class notation with attributes and methods sections

subsections.title: Objects: Runtime Instances
keyPoints: Object as runtime instance of a class
Object identity: each object is distinct
Object state: current values of all attributes
Object lifecycle: creation, use, destruction
Multiple objects from same class with different states
examples: Three BANK_ACCOUNT objects for Alice, Bob, and Carol with different balances
Multiple POINT objects representing vertices of a polygon
Student objects in a course management system, each with unique data
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Object diagram showing multiple instances of same class with different attribute values, linked to class definition

subsections.title: Encapsulation: Information Hiding
keyPoints: Encapsulation as bundling data with operations that manipulate it
Information hiding: separating interface from implementation
Public interface vs. private implementation details
Access control: public, private, protected visibility
Benefits: reduced coupling, easier maintenance, enforced invariants
examples: BANK_ACCOUNT: balance is private, accessed only through deposit/withdraw methods
STACK: internal array hidden, only push/pop/top operations exposed
DATE: internal representation (Julian day number) hidden behind day/month/year interface
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Conceptual diagram showing object boundary with public interface (visible) and private implementation (hidden)

exercises: Design a BOOK class for a library system: identify appropriate attributes and methods
Explain why making all attributes public would violate encapsulation and harm quality attributes

subsections.title: Eiffel: A Language for Quality Software
keyPoints: Eiffel designed specifically for software engineering principles
Strong support for Design by Contract (preview of future lectures)
Clear, readable syntax emphasizing concepts over syntax tricks
Multiple inheritance, genericity, and other advanced features
Concepts learned in Eiffel transfer to any OO language
examples: Comparison: same concept in Eiffel, Java, C++, Python
Eiffel's role in teaching: clarity and precision over popularity
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Timeline showing Eiffel's development and key design principles

subsections.title: Basic Eiffel Class Structure
keyPoints: Class declaration: class CLASS_NAME
Feature clauses for grouping related features
Attributes declared with type annotations
Methods (routines) with signatures and implementations
Creation procedures for object initialization
Syntax conventions: uppercase class names, lowercase feature names
examples: Simple POINT class in Eiffel with x, y attributes and distance method
COUNTER class with increment, decrement, and reset operations
RECTANGLE class with width, height, and area calculation
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Annotated Eiffel code example with callouts explaining each syntactic element

subsections.title: Reading Eiffel Code: A First Example
keyPoints: Feature visibility: exported vs. hidden features
Type declarations and type safety
Assignment and method calls
Object creation syntax
Comments and documentation style
examples: Complete BANK_ACCOUNT class in Eiffel with deposit, withdraw, balance query
Client code creating and using BANK_ACCOUNT objects
Demonstration of encapsulation through feature export control
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Side-by-side comparison of Eiffel class definition and corresponding object interactions

exercises: Read provided Eiffel CIRCLE class and identify attributes, methods, and creation procedure
Sketch how you would implement a TEMPERATURE class in Eiffel with Celsius and Fahrenheit conversions
